```{python}
    return summary.select("group", "ranking", "recall", "recall_low", "recall_high", "precision", "lift"), diffs, boots

TUNING_METRICS = {"average_precision": "max", "roc_auc": "max", "log_loss": "min", "recall_top_3pct": "max"}

def nested_rolling(spec, grid, data=None, target="y_12m", window=1, test_cohorts=TEST_COHORTS, metric="average_precision",
                   grid_by_cohort=None):
    """Rolling test with tuning nested inside: for each test cohort, choose the grid setting by inner
    cross-validation on the training cohorts, refit it on all of them, and score the test cohort.
    grid_by_cohort optionally gives a different grid for each test cohort."""
    data = frame if data is None else data
    preds, timing, tuning = [], [], []
    for T in test_cohorts:
        g = grid_by_cohort[T] if grid_by_cohort else grid
        train = data.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(spec["train_start"], T - window) & pl.col(target).is_not_null())
        start = perf_counter()
        tbl = tune(spec, g, train, target=target).with_columns(test_cohort=pl.lit(T))
        tune_seconds = perf_counter() - start
        col = pl.col(metric).fill_nan(None)
        best = tbl.sort(col, descending=TUNING_METRICS[metric] == "max", nulls_last=True)["params"][0]
        model_params, run_params = split_params(g[[str(x) for x in g].index(best)])
        chosen = {**spec, **run_params, "model": clone(spec["model"]).set_params(**model_params)}
        p, tm = rolling_test(chosen, data, target, window, [T])
        preds.append(p)
        timing.append(tm.with_columns(chosen_params=pl.lit(best), tuning_seconds=pl.lit(tune_seconds)))
        tuning.append(tbl)
    return pl.concat(preds), pl.concat(timing), pl.concat(tuning)

CACHE_DIR = Path("model_cache")
CACHE_VERSION = 1   # raise to refit everything after a change to the validation code
RERUN = False       # True refits every model instead of reading the cache

def cached_nested(spec, grid, **kw):
    """nested_rolling, saved to disk under a key built from everything that defines the run."""
    key_parts = [CACHE_VERSION, spec["name"], repr(spec["model"]), spec["scaled"], spec.get("splines"),
                 spec.get("subsample"), spec["features"], spec["train_start"], [str(g) for g in grid],
                 sorted((k, str(v)) for k, v in kw.items())]
    if spec.get("drop_empty"):
        key_parts.append(("drop_empty", True))   # appended only when set, so other keys are unchanged
    key = hashlib.sha1(json.dumps(key_parts, default=str).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
    paths = {part: CACHE_DIR / f"{key}_{part}.parquet" for part in ("preds", "timing", "tuning")}
    if not RERUN and all(p.exists() for p in paths.values()):
        return tuple(pl.read_parquet(paths[part]) for part in ("preds", "timing", "tuning"))
    result = nested_rolling(spec, grid, **kw)
    CACHE_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for part, df in zip(("preds", "timing", "tuning"), result):
        df.write_parquet(paths[part])
    return result
```

### Checking the Validation Code

Before any real model goes through this code, two checks make sure it measures what it should. The first runs a "model" that simply returns each donor's prior-year giving through the rolling test, which has to reproduce the prior-year bar from the Benchmarks section exactly. The second fits a logistic regression on prior-year giving alone, through the full scale-sensitive pipeline. A positive coefficient on a single increasing feature cannot change the order of donors, so its recall has to match the bar too, and its fitted coefficient has to be positive. A third run exercises the tuning code on the same model.

```{python}
#| label: harness-checks

from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

class PassThrough(ClassifierMixin, BaseEstimator):
    """Returns the first feature as the score, to check the validation code end to end."""
    def fit(self, X, y):
        self.classes_ = np.array([0, 1])
        return self
    def predict_proba(self, X):
        return np.column_stack([-X[:, 0], X[:, 0]])

check_specs = {
    "pass-through prior-year giving": {"name": "pass-through prior-year giving", "model": PassThrough(),
                                       "scaled": False, "features": ["prior_total"], "train_start": 2021},
    "logistic regression, prior-year giving only": {"name": "logistic regression, prior-year giving only",
                                                    "model": LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000),
                                                    "scaled": True, "features": ["prior_total"], "train_start": 2021},
}
check_runs = {name: rolling_test(spec) for name, spec in check_specs.items()}
check_summary, check_diffs, _ = evaluate_models({name: preds for name, (preds, _) in check_runs.items()})

# both checks rank donors exactly as the prior-year bar does, in every group
for g in ("all eligible", "never major", "no contact", "no contact, never major"):
    rows = {r["ranking"]: r for r in check_summary.filter(pl.col("group") == g).iter_rows(named=True)}
    for name in check_specs:
        for col in ("recall", "recall_low", "recall_high"):
            assert abs(rows[name][col] - rows["prior-year giving"][col]) < 1e-12, (g, name, col)

# the fitted logistic regressions all have a positive slope on prior-year giving
lr_check = check_specs["logistic regression, prior-year giving only"]
slopes = []
for T in TEST_COHORTS:
    tr = frame.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(2021, T - 1))
    X_tr, cols = design(tr, lr_check["features"])
    est = build(lr_check, cols).fit(X_tr, tr["y_12m"].cast(pl.Int8).to_numpy())
    slopes.append(float(est[-1].coef_[0, 0]))
assert all(s > 0 for s in slopes)

# scoring switches both contact flags off, including for the donors who had them on
test_rows = frame.filter(pl.col("t").is_in(TEST_COHORTS))
flags_on = int(test_rows.select(pl.any_horizontal(TRAINING_ONLY)).to_series().sum())
X_flags, _ = design(scoring_view(test_rows), TRAINING_ONLY)
assert flags_on > 0 and np.nansum(X_flags) == 0

# the tuning code runs on the same model, inside the FY2021 to FY2023 training cohorts
tune_check = tune(lr_check, [{"C": c} for c in (0.01, 1.0, 100.0)], frame.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(2021, 2023)))

check_timing = pl.concat([timing for _, timing in check_runs.values()])
show(check_summary.filter(pl.col("group").is_in(["all eligible", "never major"])),
     pct_cols=["recall", "recall_low", "recall_high", "precision"],
     caption="Validation code checks: both check models reproduce the prior-year bar")
```

```{python}
#| label: harness-check-tables

show(check_timing.with_columns(pl.col("fit_seconds", "predict_seconds").round(3)),
     caption="Rolling test for the two check models: training data and run time by test cohort")
```

```{python}
#| label: tune-check-table

show(tune_check.with_columns(pl.exclude("params").round(4)),
     caption="Tuning code check: inner cross-validation of the logistic regression on prior-year giving, FY2021 to FY2023 cohorts")
```

Both checks pass. The pass-through scores and the logistic regression scores give exactly the prior-year bar's recall and intervals in all four groups (all eligible, never major, and the two no-contact pools), and the logistic regression's slope on prior-year giving is positive in every training window (`{python} ", ".join(f"{s:.2f}" for s in slopes)`). So the design matrix, the pipeline, the rolling windows, and the scoring all line up with the Benchmarks section. A separate check confirms that scoring switches the contact flags off for all `{python} n(flags_on)` test-cohort donors who were contacted or held out. The timing table shows the training data each test cohort gets: `{python} n(check_timing["training_converters"][0])` converters for FY2022, rising to `{python} n(check_timing["training_converters"][-1])` for FY2024 when only FY2021 onward is used. The tuning table shows the four inner measures for three settings of the regularization strength. With one feature the ranking cannot change, so average precision, ROC AUC, and recall are identical across the settings, and only log loss responds, because stronger regularization pulls the predicted probabilities toward the average. This is a first sign that the tuning measures can disagree: the three ranking measures cannot tell these settings apart, while log loss can.

### Screening Model Families

The screen fits every model family that can rank donors, so that no family is ruled out before it has been tried. Each one gets the same inputs and the same treatment:

- **Features.** Every feature in the registry except constituent type (a sensitivity check only): the group EDA's "use" and "test" features, the engineered features, and the two contact flags for training.
- **Training window.** FY2021 onward, so each test cohort trains on the FY2021 cohort through the cohort before it.
- **Light tuning.** A small grid of each family's most important settings, usually two to six, including class weighting where the model supports it. The setting is chosen separately for each test cohort by inner cross-validation on its training cohorts, using average precision. Comparing tuning measures is left to the tuning step.
- **Slow models.** k-nearest neighbors and the kernel support vector machine scale badly with the number of rows, so they are trained on every converter plus a random 10% of non-converters. They still score every donor in the test cohort.

The fitted results are saved to disk and reused when the notebook is rendered again, keyed on each model's settings, features, and grid, so a change to any of them forces a refit. The run times reported below are the times recorded when the models were actually fit.

```{python}
#| label: screen-specs

from catboost import CatBoostClassifier
from imblearn.ensemble import BalancedRandomForestClassifier
from interpret.glassbox import ExplainableBoostingClassifier
from lightgbm import LGBMClassifier
from sklearn.discriminant_analysis import LinearDiscriminantAnalysis, QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis
from sklearn.ensemble import (AdaBoostClassifier, ExtraTreesClassifier, HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
                              RandomForestClassifier)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.svm import SVC, LinearSVC
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

SCREEN_FEATURES = [f for f, (_, status, _) in FEATURES.items() if status != "sensitivity only"]
BALANCED = [None, "balanced"]

def screen_spec(name, family, model, scaled, grid, **extra):
    return {"name": name, "family": family, "model": model, "scaled": scaled, "features": SCREEN_FEATURES,
            "train_start": 2021, "grid": grid, **extra}

def product(**options):
    # every combination of the listed settings, as a list of parameter dicts
    keys = list(options)
    return [dict(zip(keys, combo)) for combo in itertools.product(*options.values())]

SCREEN = [
    # linear and probabilistic
    screen_spec("logistic regression (L2)", "linear", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000), True,
                product(C=[0.01, 0.1, 1.0], class_weight=BALANCED)),
    screen_spec("logistic regression (L1)", "linear", LogisticRegression(solver="saga", l1_ratio=1.0, max_iter=2000), True,
                product(C=[0.01, 0.1, 1.0])),
    screen_spec("logistic regression (elastic net)", "linear",
                LogisticRegression(solver="saga", l1_ratio=0.5, max_iter=2000), True, product(C=[0.01, 0.1, 1.0])),
    screen_spec("logistic regression with splines", "linear", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000), True,
                product(C=[0.01, 0.1, 1.0]), splines=True),
    screen_spec("linear discriminant analysis", "linear", LinearDiscriminantAnalysis(solver="lsqr"), True,
                product(shrinkage=[None, "auto"])),
    # shrinkage keeps the converters' covariance estimable when a fold has fewer converters than features
    screen_spec("quadratic discriminant analysis", "probabilistic", QuadraticDiscriminantAnalysis(solver="eigen"), True,
                product(shrinkage=["auto", 0.5, 0.9])),
    screen_spec("naive Bayes", "probabilistic", GaussianNB(), True, product(var_smoothing=[1e-9, 1e-6, 1e-3])),
    # distance and margin
    screen_spec("k-nearest neighbors", "distance and margin", KNeighborsClassifier(n_jobs=-1), True,
                product(n_neighbors=[25, 100, 300]), subsample=0.10),
    screen_spec("linear support vector machine", "distance and margin", LinearSVC(max_iter=5000), True,
                product(C=[0.01, 0.1, 1.0], class_weight=BALANCED)),
    screen_spec("kernel support vector machine", "distance and margin", SVC(kernel="rbf"), True,
                product(C=[0.1, 1.0, 10.0], class_weight=["balanced"]), subsample=0.10),
    # single tree and bagging
    screen_spec("decision tree", "single tree", DecisionTreeClassifier(min_samples_leaf=100, random_state=SEED), False,
                product(max_depth=[3, 5, 8], class_weight=BALANCED)),
    screen_spec("random forest", "bagging", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED), False,
                product(min_samples_leaf=[10, 50], class_weight=[None, "balanced_subsample"])),
    screen_spec("extra trees", "bagging", ExtraTreesClassifier(n_estimators=300, n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED), False,
                product(min_samples_leaf=[10, 50], class_weight=[None, "balanced_subsample"])),
    screen_spec("balanced random forest", "bagging",
                BalancedRandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, sampling_strategy="all", replacement=True,
                                               bootstrap=False, n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED), False,
                product(min_samples_leaf=[1, 10, 50])),
    # boosting
    screen_spec("LightGBM", "boosting",
                LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, min_child_samples=50, verbose=-1, random_state=SEED), False,
                product(num_leaves=[7, 31], scale_pos_weight=[1, 10])),
    screen_spec("histogram gradient boosting", "boosting",
                HistGradientBoostingClassifier(max_iter=300, learning_rate=0.05, early_stopping=False, random_state=SEED), False,
                product(max_leaf_nodes=[7, 31], class_weight=BALANCED),
                # its binning fails on a column with no observed values, such as soft credits before
                # FY t when the FY2021 cohort is the only training cohort
                drop_empty=True),
    screen_spec("XGBoost", "boosting",
                XGBClassifier(n_estimators=300, learning_rate=0.05, tree_method="hist", n_jobs=-1, random_state=SEED), False,
                product(max_depth=[3, 6], scale_pos_weight=[1, 10])),
    screen_spec("CatBoost", "boosting",
                CatBoostClassifier(iterations=500, learning_rate=0.05, verbose=0, allow_writing_files=False, random_seed=SEED), False,
                product(depth=[4, 6], scale_pos_weight=[1, 10])),
    screen_spec("AdaBoost", "boosting", AdaBoostClassifier(random_state=SEED), True,
                product(n_estimators=[50, 200, 500])),
    screen_spec("explainable boosting machine", "boosting", ExplainableBoostingClassifier(random_state=SEED), False,
                product(interactions=[0, 10])),
    # neural network
    screen_spec("neural network (MLP)", "neural network",
                MLPClassifier(early_stopping=True, max_iter=300, random_state=SEED), True,
                product(hidden_layer_sizes=[(32,), (64, 32)], alpha=[1e-4, 1e-2])),
]
assert len({s["name"] for s in SCREEN}) == len(SCREEN)
```

```{python}
with_scores = test_scored

    for m in screen_preds
]).sort("recall_all", descending=True)
st = {r["model"]: r for r in screen_table.iter_rows(named=True)}

# which models clear each bar under the 95% paired rule
clears = {

    for g in ("all eligible", "never major", "no contact") for b in ("prior-year giving", "former major or $500")
}
bar_rows = pl.DataFrame([
    {"model": b, "family": "baseline", "recall_all": s_all[b]["recall"], "recall_never_major": s_never[b]["recall"],

    for b in ("prior-year giving", "former major or $500")
])
```

The screen gives a clear answer for all eligible donors and a weak one for never-major donors.

**All eligible donors.** `{python} len(clears[("all eligible", "prior-year giving")])` of the `{python} len(SCREEN)` models beat the prior-year ranking under the 95% paired rule: `{python} ", ".join(clears[("all eligible", "prior-year giving")])`. The best reach `{python} pct(st["logistic regression (L1)"]["recall_all"])` recall at 1,000 against `{python} pct(ba["prior-year giving"]["recall"])` for the ranking, a gain of `{python} pp(st["logistic regression (L1)"]["gain_vs_prior_year"], 1)` points (95% interval `{python} pp(st["logistic regression (L1)"]["gain_low"], 1)` to `{python} pp(st["logistic regression (L1)"]["gain_high"], 1)`) for the L1 logistic regression. All of them also clear the former major or $500 rule. On the test cohorts that is about `{python} n(st["logistic regression (L1)"]["gain_vs_prior_year"] * by_cohort["converters"].sum())` more of the `{python} n(by_cohort["converters"].sum())` converters on the lists over three years. The gain is larger on the no-contact pool (`{python} pct(s_nc["logistic regression (L1)"]["recall"])` against `{python} pct(s_nc["prior-year giving"]["recall"])`), but that pool rests on far fewer converters and its paired interval just reaches zero.

**Never-major donors.** No model clears the bar. The L1 logistic regression comes closest at `{python} pct(st["logistic regression (L1)"]["recall_never_major"])` against `{python} pct(bn["prior-year giving"]["recall"])`, a gain of `{python} pp(st["logistic regression (L1)"]["never_major_gain"], 1)` points with an interval from `{python} pp(st["logistic regression (L1)"]["never_major_gain_low"], 1)` to `{python} pp(st["logistic regression (L1)"]["never_major_gain_high"], 1)`. Most models do worse than the ranking for these donors. With `{python} n(test_never["y"].sum())` never-major converters across the three test cohorts, the screen cannot separate a small real gain from noise here, and some of the models' gain for all donors comes from ranking former major donors better.

**Average precision.** The best models nearly triple the prior-year ranking's average precision (`{python} f'{st["logistic regression (L1)"]["test_average_precision"]:.2f}'` against `{python} f'{screen_display.filter(pl.col("model") == "prior-year giving")["test_average_precision"][0]:.2f}'`), a much larger relative gain than in recall at 1,000. Average precision rewards placing converters near the very top of the list, and the prior-year ranking already reaches most converters by position 1,000, just not as early. A model that puts likely converters in the first hundred names is more useful to an officer working down the list, even when recall at 1,000 moves less.

**What does not work.** The flexible tree models do worst relative to their reputation. LightGBM falls below the bar (`{python} pct(st["LightGBM"]["recall_all"])`), and histogram gradient boosting, the single decision tree, the neural network, and quadratic discriminant analysis also land below the prior-year ranking. XGBoost and CatBoost sit just above it but do not clear it. With only `{python} n(check_timing.filter(pl.col("model") == "pass-through prior-year giving")["training_converters"][0])` to `{python} n(check_timing.filter(pl.col("model") == "pass-through prior-year giving")["training_converters"][-1])` converters in the training cohorts, models that can carve the data into many small regions fit noise, and the tuning sometimes chose the larger trees (see the settings table). The strongest signals, prior-year giving and former major status, act in a steady, mostly one-directional way, which suits penalized linear models. The two models trained on a 10% sample of non-converters, k-nearest neighbors and the kernel support vector machine, land in the middle of the pack (`{python} pct(st["k-nearest neighbors"]["recall_all"])` and `{python} pct(st["kernel support vector machine"]["recall_all"])`) without clearing the bar.

**Run time.** Most models took a few minutes for the whole screen. The L1 and elastic net logistic regressions took `{python} f'{tt_["logistic regression (L1)"]["total_minutes"]:.0f}'` and `{python} f'{tt_["logistic regression (elastic net)"]["total_minutes"]:.0f}'` minutes because of the solver they need, while the L2 version took `{python} f'{tt_["logistic regression (L2)"]["total_minutes"]:.0f}'` minutes for nearly the same recall. AdaBoost took `{python} f'{tt_["AdaBoost"]["total_minutes"]:.0f}'` minutes. Once fit, every model scores a cohort of 33,000 donors in a few seconds or less.

A caution applies to the whole table. With 21 models compared on the same 134 converters, the top of the ranking is partly luck, which is why the shortlist below carries families forward rather than a single winner, and why the FY2025 check comes only after the final choice. Still, the result does not hinge on one model: four different logistic regressions, AdaBoost, and the explainable boosting machine all land between `{python} pct(min(st[m]["recall_all"] for m in clears[("all eligible", "prior-year giving")]))` and `{python} pct(max(st[m]["recall_all"] for m in clears[("all eligible", "prior-year giving")]))`.

### Shortlist

Four models move on to feature engineering, the training window comparison, and full tuning:

- **Logistic regression with an L2 penalty.** It clears both bars and is the fastest of the logistic regressions.
- **Logistic regression with an L1 penalty.** It comes closest to a gain for never-major donors. From here on it uses the liblinear solver, which fits the same L1-penalized model much faster than the saga solver used in the screen (liblinear also applies a light penalty to the intercept, which does not change the ranking in any meaningful way).
- **Explainable boosting machine.** It clears both bars, ties the logistic regressions on average precision, and is built from one curve per feature plus a few pairwise interactions, so it can show each donor's main drivers, which the business problem asks for in the working queue.
- **XGBoost.** It is the strongest of the flexible tree-boosting libraries and does not clear the bar here. It stays on the list to test whether stronger regularization in the tuning step fixes the overfitting the screen suggests, since that would be the main reason to prefer a more flexible model.

The elastic net and spline versions of logistic regression match the L1 version for all donors and do worse for never-major donors, so they add nothing. AdaBoost ties the leaders for all donors, but it is slower, weaker for never-major donors, and an additive boosted model like the explainable boosting machine without that model's interpretability. The other models do not clear the bar.

### Feature Engineering

The screen used every feature. This step asks which groups of features actually help, by refitting the four shortlisted models on nested feature sets and comparing them on the same resamples:

| Feature set | What it contains |
|---|---|
| Group EDA use list | The group EDA's "use" features and the two contact flags for training |
| Use + test | Adds the features the group EDA expected to add little: recency, upgrade and additional gifts, soft credits in FY t, solicitation, Passport, state, and spouse on file |
| Use + engineered | Adds the engineered features from the Data Preparation section instead |
| All | Everything, the screen's feature set |
| All without solicitation and Passport | Everything except the engagement features, which only exist from FY2021 |

The comparisons answer three questions. Do the engineered features help (use + engineered against the use list)? Do the group EDA's "test" features help (use + test against the use list)? And do solicitation and Passport add anything once everything else is known (all against all without them)? The last question is one the business problem asks directly. Constituent type is tried once, added to the full set for the L2 logistic regression, as the sensitivity check the team agreed on.

```{python}
#| label: feature-sets

def by_status(*statuses):
    return [f for f, (_, status, _) in FEATURES.items() if status in statuses]

ENGAGEMENT = [f for f, (group, _, _) in FEATURES.items() if group in ("solicitation", "Passport")]
ALL_FEATURES = by_status("use", "test", "engineered", "training only")
assert ALL_FEATURES == SCREEN_FEATURES   # same list and order, so the screen's fits are reused from the cache
FEATURE_SETS = {
    "group EDA use list": by_status("use", "training only"),
    "use + test": by_status("use", "test", "training only"),
    "use + engineered": by_status("use", "engineered", "training only"),
    "all": ALL_FEATURES,
    "all without solicitation and Passport": [f for f in ALL_FEATURES if f not in ENGAGEMENT],
}

screen_by_name = {s["name"]: s for s in SCREEN}
SHORTLIST = {
    "logistic regression (L2)": screen_by_name["logistic regression (L2)"],
    "logistic regression (L1)": screen_spec("logistic regression (L1)", "linear",
                                            LogisticRegression(solver="liblinear", l1_ratio=1.0, max_iter=2000), True,
                                            product(C=[0.01, 0.1, 1.0])),
    "explainable boosting machine": screen_by_name["explainable boosting machine"],
    "XGBoost": screen_by_name["XGBoost"],
}

feature_runs = {
    (m, fs): cached_nested({**spec, "features": feats}, spec["grid"])
    for m, spec in SHORTLIST.items() for fs, feats in FEATURE_SETS.items()
}
# sensitivity check: constituent type added to the full set, for the L2 logistic regression only
l2 = SHORTLIST["logistic regression (L2)"]
feature_runs[("logistic regression (L2)", "all + constituent type")] = cached_nested(
    {**l2, "features": [*ALL_FEATURES, "type_group"]}, l2["grid"])
```

```{python}
#| label: feature-results

fs_preds = {f"{m} | {fs}": run[0] for (m, fs), run in feature_runs.items()}
fs_summary, fs_bar_diffs, fs_boots = evaluate_models(fs_preds)

fs_with = test_scored
for name, p in fs_preds.items():
    fs_with = fs_with.join(p.rename({"score": f"score__{name}"}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")

def fs_row(g, name):
    return fs_summary.filter((pl.col("group") == g) & (pl.col("ranking") == name)).row(0, named=True)

fs_table = pl.DataFrame([
    {"model": m, "feature_set": fs,
     "features": len(FEATURE_SETS[fs]) if fs in FEATURE_SETS else len(ALL_FEATURES) + 1,
     "recall_all": fs_row("all eligible", f"{m} | {fs}")["recall"],
     "recall_never_major": fs_row("never major", f"{m} | {fs}")["recall"],
     "recall_no_contact": fs_row("no contact", f"{m} | {fs}")["recall"],
     "test_average_precision": test_average_precision(f"score__{m} | {fs}", fs_with)}
    for (m, fs) in feature_runs
])
ft = {(r["model"], r["feature_set"]): r for r in fs_table.iter_rows(named=True)}
fd = {(r["group"], r["model"]): r for r in fs_bar_diffs.filter(pl.col("versus") == "prior-year giving").iter_rows(named=True)}
show(fs_table.with_columns(pl.col("test_average_precision").round(3)),
     pct_cols=["recall_all", "recall_never_major", "recall_no_contact"],
     caption="Shortlisted models on each feature set: recall at 1,000 on the FY2022 to FY2024 test cohorts")
```

```{python}
#| label: feature-effects

# each question is a paired difference between two feature sets of the same model
QUESTIONS = {
    "engineered features": ("use + engineered", "group EDA use list"),
    "group EDA test features": ("use + test", "group EDA use list"),
    "solicitation and Passport": ("all", "all without solicitation and Passport"),
    "everything beyond the use list": ("all", "group EDA use list"),
}
effect_rows = []
for m in SHORTLIST:
    for q, (a, b) in QUESTIONS.items():
        row = {"model": m, "question": q}
        for g, label in (("all eligible", "all"), ("never major", "never_major")):
            diff = paired_difference(fs_boots[g], f"{m} | {a}", f"{m} | {b}")
            row |= {f"{label}_gain": 100 * diff["difference"], f"{label}_low": 100 * diff["low"],
                    f"{label}_high": 100 * diff["high"]}
        effect_rows.append(row)
sens = paired_difference(fs_boots["all eligible"], "logistic regression (L2) | all + constituent type",
                         "logistic regression (L2) | all")
effect_rows.append({"model": "logistic regression (L2)", "question": "constituent type (sensitivity)",
                    "all_gain": 100 * sens["difference"], "all_low": 100 * sens["low"], "all_high": 100 * sens["high"]})
effects = pl.DataFrame(effect_rows)
ef_ = {(r["model"], r["question"]): r for r in effects.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(effects.with_columns(pl.exclude("model", "question").round(1)),
     caption="What each feature group adds: paired gain in recall at 1,000, percentage points, with 95% intervals")
```

```{python}
#| label: feature-effect-ranges

linear_ebm = ["logistic regression (L2)", "logistic regression (L1)", "explainable boosting machine"]
main_qs = ["engineered features", "group EDA test features", "solicitation and Passport", "everything beyond the use list"]
le_gains = [ef_[(m, q)]["all_gain"] for m in linear_ebm for q in main_qs]
le_excluding_zero = [(m, q) for m in linear_ebm for q in main_qs if ef_[(m, q)]["all_high"] < 0 or ef_[(m, q)]["all_low"] > 0]
engagement = [ef_[(m, "solicitation and Passport")] for m in SHORTLIST]
l1_use = fd[("all eligible", "logistic regression (L1) | group EDA use list")]
ap_use = {m: ft[(m, "group EDA use list")]["test_average_precision"] for m in SHORTLIST}
ap_eng = {m: ft[(m, "use + engineered")]["test_average_precision"] for m in SHORTLIST}
assert all(ap_eng[m] > ap_use[m] for m in SHORTLIST)   # the engineered features raise average precision for every model
best_never = max(fs_table.iter_rows(named=True), key=lambda r: r["recall_never_major"])
```

**Fewer features do as well or better.** For the two logistic regressions and the explainable boosting machine, the smallest set, the group EDA's use list with `{python} n(len(FEATURE_SETS["group EDA use list"]))` inputs, matches or beats every larger set. The L1 logistic regression on the use list reaches `{python} pct(ft[("logistic regression (L1)", "group EDA use list")]["recall_all"])` recall at 1,000, `{python} pp(l1_use["difference"], 1)` points above the prior-year ranking (95% interval `{python} pp(l1_use["low"], 1)` to `{python} pp(l1_use["high"], 1)`), the best result so far. For these three models, adding feature groups changes recall by between `{python} f"{min(le_gains):.1f}"` and `{python} f"{max(le_gains):+.1f}" if max(le_gains) > 0 else "0"` points, and only `{python} n(len(le_excluding_zero))` of the `{python} n(len(le_gains))` paired intervals excludes zero: the group EDA's "test" features lower the L1 model's recall by `{python} f'{-ef_[("logistic regression (L1)", "group EDA test features")]["all_gain"]:.1f}'` points (`{python} f'{ef_[("logistic regression (L1)", "group EDA test features")]["all_low"]:.1f}'` to `{python} f'{ef_[("logistic regression (L1)", "group EDA test features")]["all_high"]:.1f}'`). With few converters to learn from, each extra feature is another chance to fit noise, and the penalized models and the boosting machine do best when the inputs are the ones the EDA already found useful.

**Solicitation and Passport add nothing.** Removing them changes recall by between `{python} f'{min(e["all_gain"] for e in engagement):.1f}'` and `{python} f'{max(e["all_gain"] for e in engagement):+.1f}'` points across the four models, and every interval includes zero, for all eligible donors and for never-major donors. This answers the business problem's question about engagement and viewing: once giving history is known, they do not help find future major donors, which matches the group EDA's within-band results.

**The engineered features help a little, near the top of the list.** They do not raise recall at 1,000 for the linear models or the boosting machine, but they raise average precision for all four models, for example from `{python} f'{ap_use["explainable boosting machine"]:.3f}'` to `{python} f'{ap_eng["explainable boosting machine"]:.3f}'` for the explainable boosting machine. They move some converters higher within the list without adding converters to it.

**XGBoost is the exception.** It is the only model that gains from more inputs: the group EDA's "test" features raise its recall by `{python} f'{ef_[("XGBoost", "group EDA test features")]["all_gain"]:.1f}'` points (`{python} f'{ef_[("XGBoost", "group EDA test features")]["all_low"]:.1f}'` to `{python} f'{ef_[("XGBoost", "group EDA test features")]["all_high"]:.1f}'`), and on the use list alone it does no better than the prior-year ranking (`{python} pct(ft[("XGBoost", "group EDA use list")]["recall_all"])`). A flexible tree model needs varied inputs to split on, while the linear models get most of their signal from a few monotone features. Even XGBoost's best set (`{python} pct(max(ft[("XGBoost", fs)]["recall_all"] for fs in FEATURE_SETS))`) stays below the best linear models.

**Constituent type** changes the L2 model's recall by `{python} f'{ef_[("logistic regression (L2)", "constituent type (sensitivity)")]["all_gain"]:.1f}'` points (`{python} f'{ef_[("logistic regression (L2)", "constituent type (sensitivity)")]["all_low"]:.1f}'` to `{python} f'{ef_[("logistic regression (L2)", "constituent type (sensitivity)")]["all_high"]:.1f}'`), so leaving it out of the main model, as the team agreed, costs nothing.

**Never-major donors.** No model and feature set clears the bar. The best is `{python} best_never["model"]` on the `{python} best_never["feature_set"]` set at `{python} pct(best_never["recall_never_major"])`, against `{python} pct(bn["prior-year giving"]["recall"])` for the ranking.

A caution: choosing a feature set by its result on the test cohorts is itself part of model selection, so the winning set's advantage is probably a little overstated. The differences between sets are small next to their intervals, so the safer reading is that the extra features neither help nor hurt much, and the simplest set does as well as any. The FY2025 check at the end remains the honest test of whatever is chosen.

From here on, the two logistic regressions and the explainable boosting machine use the group EDA's use list, the smallest set and the best or tied for best for each of them. XGBoost keeps the use + test set, since it is the one model that gains from the extra inputs. The use + engineered set remains the alternative if placing converters near the very top of the list turns out to matter more than recall at 1,000.

### Training Window

So far every model has trained on the FY2021 cohort onward, which gives the FY2022 test only `{python} n(check_timing["training_converters"][0])` converters to learn from and the FY2024 test `{python} n(check_timing["training_converters"][-1])`. The legacy-era cohorts add hundreds more, and the chosen feature sets are almost entirely giving history, which exists in every era. The open question is whether older donors behave enough like recent ones for their outcomes to help. The sustainer share was much lower before FY2014, and the legacy system recorded sustainers' payments differently, so older years could also mislead a model.

Three training windows are compared, each ending in the cohort before the test cohort:

- **FY2021 onward**, the window used so far.
- **FY2014 onward**, roughly when sustaining took off (the sustainer share rose from about a quarter of donors to more than half over the following years), so donors look more like today's.
- **FY1999 onward**, all of the complete legacy history.

Everything else stays fixed: the four shortlisted models with their chosen feature sets, nested tuning, and the FY2022 to FY2024 test cohorts. Features that do not exist in older cohorts (soft credits before FY t, and the engagement features in XGBoost's set) are missing there, as set up in the Data Preparation section.

Before running the comparison I set a rule for one follow-up, so that the results would not decide whether to look further. If the FY1999 window helps across the board, it is used as it is. If it hurts across the board, the better of the shorter windows is used. If the results are mixed, meaning the long window helps for some groups or models and hurts for others, or the FY2014 window beats both, then older years carry signal but have drifted, and a version of the FY1999 window that weights recent cohorts more heavily is tested as well.

```{python}
#| label: window-runs

CHOSEN_SETS = {"logistic regression (L2)": "group EDA use list", "logistic regression (L1)": "group EDA use list",
               "explainable boosting machine": "group EDA use list", "XGBoost": "use + test"}
WINDOWS = {"FY2021 onward": 2021, "FY2014 onward": 2014, "FY1999 onward": 1999}

def chosen_spec(m, train_start=2021):
    return {**SHORTLIST[m], "features": FEATURE_SETS[CHOSEN_SETS[m]], "train_start": train_start}

window_runs = {
    (m, w): cached_nested(chosen_spec(m, start), SHORTLIST[m]["grid"])
    for m in SHORTLIST for w, start in WINDOWS.items()
}
```

```{python}
#| label: window-results

win_preds = {f"{m} | {w}": run[0] for (m, w), run in window_runs.items()}
win_summary, win_bar_diffs, win_boots = evaluate_models(win_preds)
win_with = test_scored
for name, p in win_preds.items():
    win_with = win_with.join(p.rename({"score": f"score__{name}"}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")

def win_row(g, name):
    return win_summary.filter((pl.col("group") == g) & (pl.col("ranking") == name)).row(0, named=True)

win_table = pl.DataFrame([
    {"model": m, "window": w,
     "training_converters_FY2024_test": int(run[1].filter(pl.col("test_cohort") == 2024)["training_converters"][0]),
     "recall_all": win_row("all eligible", f"{m} | {w}")["recall"],
     "recall_never_major": win_row("never major", f"{m} | {w}")["recall"],
     "recall_no_contact": win_row("no contact", f"{m} | {w}")["recall"],
     "test_average_precision": test_average_precision(f"score__{m} | {w}", win_with),
     "total_minutes": float((run[1]["tuning_seconds"] + run[1]["fit_seconds"] + run[1]["predict_seconds"]).sum() / 60)}
    for (m, w), run in window_runs.items()
])
wt = {(r["model"], r["window"]): r for r in win_table.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(win_table.with_columns(pl.col("test_average_precision").round(3), pl.col("total_minutes").round(1)),
     pct_cols=["recall_all", "recall_never_major", "recall_no_contact"],
     caption="Shortlisted models trained on three windows: recall at 1,000 on the FY2022 to FY2024 test cohorts")
```

```{python}
#| label: window-effects

WINDOW_PAIRS = [("FY2014 onward", "FY2021 onward"), ("FY1999 onward", "FY2021 onward"), ("FY1999 onward", "FY2014 onward")]
win_effect_rows = []
for m in SHORTLIST:
    for a, b in WINDOW_PAIRS:
        row = {"model": m, "comparison": f"{a} minus {b}"}
        for g, label in (("all eligible", "all"), ("never major", "never_major")):
            diff = paired_difference(win_boots[g], f"{m} | {a}", f"{m} | {b}")
            row |= {f"{label}_gain": 100 * diff["difference"], f"{label}_low": 100 * diff["low"],
                    f"{label}_high": 100 * diff["high"]}
        win_effect_rows.append(row)
win_effects = pl.DataFrame(win_effect_rows)
we = {(r["model"], r["comparison"]): r for r in win_effects.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(win_effects.with_columns(pl.exclude("model", "comparison").round(1)),
     caption="Paired differences between training windows in recall at 1,000, percentage points, with 95% intervals")
```

```{python}
#| label: window-ranges

pair_2014 = "FY2014 onward minus FY2021 onward"
pair_1999 = "FY1999 onward minus FY2021 onward"
pair_99_14 = "FY1999 onward minus FY2014 onward"
def gain_range(pair, col):
    vals = [we[(m, pair)][col] for m in SHORTLIST]
    return min(vals), max(vals)
wd = {(r["group"], r["model"]): r for r in win_bar_diffs.filter(pl.col("versus") == "prior-year giving").iter_rows(named=True)}
all_clear = all(wd[("all eligible", f"{m} | {w}")]["low"] > 0 for m in SHORTLIST for w in WINDOWS)
never_2014_not_worse = all(wt[(m, "FY2014 onward")]["recall_never_major"] >= wt[(m, "FY2021 onward")]["recall_never_major"] for m in SHORTLIST)
ap_2014_higher = all(wt[(m, "FY2014 onward")]["test_average_precision"] > wt[(m, "FY2021 onward")]["test_average_precision"] for m in SHORTLIST)
assert all_clear and never_2014_not_worse and ap_2014_higher
extra_converters = wt[("logistic regression (L2)", "FY1999 onward")]["training_converters_FY2024_test"] - wt[("logistic regression (L2)", "FY2014 onward")]["training_converters_FY2024_test"]

def fmt_range(lo, hi):
    return f"{lo:.1f} to {hi:+.1f}" if hi > 0 else f"{lo:.1f} to 0"
```

**For all eligible donors the window makes little difference.** Moving from FY2021 onward to FY2014 onward changes recall by `{python} fmt_range(*gain_range(pair_2014, "all_gain"))` points across the four models, and moving to FY1999 onward by `{python} fmt_range(*gain_range(pair_1999, "all_gain"))`, with every paired interval including zero. All twelve combinations of model and window still beat the prior-year ranking under the 95% rule.

**Longer windows lean toward helping never-major donors and the top of the list.** With FY2014 onward, never-major recall is the same as or higher than with FY2021 onward for all four models (`{python} fmt_range(*gain_range(pair_2014, "never_major_gain"))` points), and average precision is higher for all four. None of these never-major gains is clearly above zero, though. The largest interval lower bound is `{python} f'{max(we[(m, pair_2014)]["never_major_low"] for m in SHORTLIST):.1f}'`, and no model and window clears the never-major bar.

**Going back to FY1999 adds nothing beyond FY2014.** The extra fifteen years bring `{python} n(extra_converters)` more converters to the FY2024 training set, yet against FY2014 onward they change recall by `{python} fmt_range(*gain_range(pair_99_14, "all_gain"))` points for all eligible donors and `{python} fmt_range(*gain_range(pair_99_14, "never_major_gain"))` for never-major donors. They also make every model slower: the L1 logistic regression took `{python} f'{wt[("logistic regression (L1)", "FY1999 onward")]["total_minutes"]:.0f}'` minutes on FY1999 onward against `{python} f'{wt[("logistic regression (L1)", "FY2014 onward")]["total_minutes"]:.0f}'` on FY2014 onward.

**Applying the rule.** The rule set before the comparison assumed the long window would clearly help or clearly hurt. Instead no window measurably differs from another, and the point estimates point different ways: the FY1999 window raises never-major recall for three models and lowers it for the L1 logistic regression, and the FY2014 window beats both other windows for two of the models. Read as written, that is the mixed case, so the weighted FY1999 window is tested as the rule requires, even though the differences it would explain are within noise.

### Weighting Recent Cohorts

The weighted version keeps all of FY1999 onward but counts recent cohorts more. Each training cohort's weight halves every *h* years counting back from the most recent training cohort, so with *h* = 6 a cohort six years older counts half as much. The half-life *h* is chosen from 3, 6, and 12 years by inner cross-validation on each test cohort's training data, like any other setting. To keep the run affordable, each model's own settings are fixed at what the unweighted FY1999 run chose for that test cohort, which were themselves chosen by inner cross-validation on the same training data, so only the half-life is tuned here. The weights apply to fitting only; every validation and test donor counts equally.

```{python}
#| label: weighted-window-runs

import ast

HALF_LIVES = [3, 6, 12]

def weighted_grid(m):
    # per test cohort: the settings the unweighted FY1999 run chose, crossed with each half-life
    chosen = window_runs[(m, "FY1999 onward")][1]
    return {int(r["test_cohort"]): [{**ast.literal_eval(r["chosen_params"]), "recency_half_life": h} for h in HALF_LIVES]
            for r in chosen.iter_rows(named=True)}

weighted_runs = {m: cached_nested(chosen_spec(m, 1999), [], grid_by_cohort=weighted_grid(m)) for m in SHORTLIST}
```

```{python}
def wtd_row(g, name):
```

The weighted window does not change the picture. Tuning chose long half-lives more often than short ones (12 years for the explainable boosting machine in every test cohort), so the weighting it settled on is mild, and the results land close to the FY2014 window: `{python} pct(min(wtd_recall))` to `{python} pct(max(wtd_recall))` recall for all eligible donors and `{python} pct(min(wtd_never))` to `{python} pct(max(wtd_never))` for never-major donors. None of the `{python} n(wtd_effects.height)` paired comparisons with the unweighted windows excludes zero, for either group. All four weighted models still beat the prior-year ranking for all eligible donors, and none clears it for never-major donors.

Taken together, the training window comparison finds no measurable effect in any direction. Adding older cohorts, with or without weighting, gives every model hundreds more converters to learn from without changing recall at 1,000 by more than the noise in 134 test converters. The most likely reason is that the strongest signals, prior-year giving and former major status, are already estimated well from the recent cohorts, and the older cohorts add more donors of the same kind rather than new information.

From here on, every model trains on the FY2014 window. The test results cannot separate the windows, so the choice rests on reasons that do not depend on them. Training on FY2021 onward leaves very few converters to learn from (`{python} n(int(frame.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(2021, 2024))["y_12m"].sum()))` in FY2021 to FY2024, only `{python} n(int(frame.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(2021, 2024) & ~pl.col("former_major"))["y_12m"].sum()))` of them never-major donors), and the tuning step would be choosing settings from inner folds with about a dozen converters each. The FY2014 window roughly triples the converters, stays within the period when sustaining became common, does at least as well as the other windows on every measure, and avoids the extra tuning setting the weighting needs. One cost is that its probabilities reflect a mix of years with different base rates, which the calibration check in the Best Model Performance section will look at. I also checked that the switch from the legacy system to Unite does not distort the giving-change features at FY2021: the share of sustainers who gave more than the year before declines smoothly through the switch rather than jumping.

### Hyperparameter Tuning

The screen and the experiments above used small grids. This step tunes the four shortlisted models properly, on the FY2014 window with each model's chosen feature set, and uses the same runs to compare the four tuning measures.

| Model | Grid |
|---|---|
| L2 logistic regression | Penalty strength C from 0.001 to 3 (eight values), with and without balanced class weights: 16 settings |
| L1 logistic regression | C from 0.003 to 1 (six values), with and without balanced class weights: 12 settings |
| Explainable boosting machine | Pairwise interactions (0, 5, or 10), learning rate (0.005 or the default 0.015), and minimum leaf size (the default 4, or 50): 12 settings |
| XGBoost | A random search of 30 settings over tree depth, learning rate, number of trees, minimum child weight, row and column subsampling, the L2 penalty, and class weighting, aimed at the stronger regularization the screen suggested it needs |

For each test cohort, every setting goes through the same grouped inner cross-validation, which records all four tuning measures. Each measure then picks its own best setting, and those picks are refit and scored on the test cohort. This shows whether the tuning measure changes the chosen setting, and whether that matters on the test cohorts.

Three rules were set before the runs:

1. **Tuning measure.** Average precision, used so far, stays the tuning measure unless another measure's picks give higher recall at 1,000 with a paired 95% interval above zero. If no measure differs measurably, average precision stays.
2. **Full tuning carries forward.** The fully tuned version of each model is used from here on whatever its test result, because the tuning happens entirely inside the training cohorts. Accepting or rejecting it based on the test cohorts would itself be selecting on the test data. Its comparison with the lightly tuned FY2014 versions is reported for information only.
3. **All four models move on** to the final comparison, where the selection rule decides between them.

```{python}
#| label: tuning-grids

def random_grid(options, n, seed=SEED):
    # n distinct settings drawn at random from the full grid of options
    full = product(**options)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    return [full[i] for i in sorted(rng.choice(len(full), size=n, replace=False))]

TUNE_GRIDS = {
    "logistic regression (L2)": product(C=[0.001, 0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0, 3.0], class_weight=BALANCED),
    "logistic regression (L1)": product(C=[0.003, 0.01, 0.03, 0.1, 0.3, 1.0], class_weight=BALANCED),
    "explainable boosting machine": product(interactions=[0, 5, 10], learning_rate=[0.005, 0.015], min_samples_leaf=[4, 50]),
    "XGBoost": random_grid({"max_depth": [2, 3, 4, 6], "learning_rate": [0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.1],
                            "n_estimators": [100, 300, 600], "min_child_weight": [1, 5, 20, 50],
                            "subsample": [0.6, 0.8, 1.0], "colsample_bytree": [0.5, 0.8, 1.0],
                            "reg_lambda": [1, 10, 50], "scale_pos_weight": [1, 10]}, n=30),
}
TUNE_START = 2014   # the training window chosen above

def pick(tbl, metric):
    # the grid setting a tuning measure prefers
    col = pl.col(metric).fill_nan(None)
    return tbl.sort(col, descending=TUNING_METRICS[metric] == "max", nulls_last=True)["params"][0]

def nested_multi(spec, grid, data=None, target="y_12m", window=1, test_cohorts=TEST_COHORTS):
    """Tune once per test cohort, then refit and score the setting each tuning measure picks.
    Returns {measure: (preds, timing)} and the tuning table."""
    data = frame if data is None else data
    out = {metric: ([], []) for metric in TUNING_METRICS}
    tuning = []
    for T in test_cohorts:
        train = data.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(spec["train_start"], T - window) & pl.col(target).is_not_null())
        start = perf_counter()
        tbl = tune(spec, grid, train, target=target).with_columns(test_cohort=pl.lit(T))
        tune_seconds = perf_counter() - start
        fitted = {}   # a setting picked by several measures is fit once
        for metric in TUNING_METRICS:
            best = pick(tbl, metric)
            if best not in fitted:
                model_params, run_params = split_params(grid[[str(g) for g in grid].index(best)])
                chosen = {**spec, **run_params, "model": clone(spec["model"]).set_params(**model_params)}
                fitted[best] = rolling_test(chosen, data, target, window, [T])
            p, tm = fitted[best]
            out[metric][0].append(p)
            out[metric][1].append(tm.with_columns(chosen_params=pl.lit(best), tuning_seconds=pl.lit(tune_seconds)))
        tuning.append(tbl)
    return {m: (pl.concat(p), pl.concat(tm)) for m, (p, tm) in out.items()}, pl.concat(tuning)

def cached_multi(spec, grid, **kw):
    """nested_multi, saved to disk like cached_nested."""
    key_parts = ["multi-measure", CACHE_VERSION, spec["name"], repr(spec["model"]), spec["scaled"], spec.get("splines"),
                 spec.get("subsample"), spec.get("drop_empty"), spec["features"], spec["train_start"],
                 [str(g) for g in grid], sorted((k, str(v)) for k, v in kw.items())]
    key = hashlib.sha1(json.dumps(key_parts, default=str).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
    paths = {f"{m}_{part}": CACHE_DIR / f"{key}_{m}_{part}.parquet" for m in TUNING_METRICS for part in ("preds", "timing")}
    paths["tuning"] = CACHE_DIR / f"{key}_tuning.parquet"
    if not RERUN and all(p.exists() for p in paths.values()):
        return ({m: (pl.read_parquet(paths[f"{m}_preds"]), pl.read_parquet(paths[f"{m}_timing"])) for m in TUNING_METRICS},
                pl.read_parquet(paths["tuning"]))
    by_metric, tuning = nested_multi(spec, grid, **kw)
    CACHE_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for m, (p, tm) in by_metric.items():
        p.write_parquet(paths[f"{m}_preds"])
        tm.write_parquet(paths[f"{m}_timing"])
    tuning.write_parquet(paths["tuning"])
    return by_metric, tuning
```

**The tuning measures disagree about settings but not about results.** The other three measures picked the same setting as average precision in only `{python} n(sum(same_picks))` of `{python} n(3 * len(same_picks))` cases (three measures, four models, three test cohorts), often choosing quite different penalties or tree shapes. Yet their picks change recall at 1,000 by `{python} fmt_range(min(m_all), max(m_all))` points against the average precision picks, and none of the paired intervals is above zero. Under the first rule, average precision stays the tuning measure. The top of the ranking is evidently insensitive to these settings: once a model has prior-year giving and former major status, the order of the first 1,000 donors barely changes across a wide range of penalties.

**Full tuning changes little next to the light grids.** Against the lightly tuned FY2014 versions, the fully tuned models differ by `{python} fmt_range(min(light_all), max(light_all))` points of recall, with every interval including zero. Under the second rule the fully tuned versions carry forward anyway, since their settings were chosen without looking at the test cohorts.

**XGBoost responded to regularization.** Tuned on average precision it chose shallow trees of depth 3 or less in `{python} n(sum(d <= 3 for d in xgb_depths))` of the 3 test cohorts (depths `{python} ", ".join(str(d) for d in xgb_depths)`), and its average precision on the test cohorts rose from `{python} f"{xgb_ap_light:.3f}"` with the light grid to `{python} f'{tr_[("XGBoost", "average precision")]["test_average_precision"]:.3f}'`, close to the other three models. That supports the screen's reading that its earlier weakness came from overfitting rather than from the algorithm.

**Where the four models stand.** Fully tuned on the FY2014 window, the four models reach `{python} pct(min(tuned_all))` to `{python} pct(max(tuned_all))` recall at 1,000 for all eligible donors, `{python} f"{min(tuned_gain):.1f}"` to `{python} f"{max(tuned_gain):.1f}"` points above the prior-year ranking, and all four clear the bar under the 95% rule. For never-major donors they reach `{python} pct(min(tuned_never)) if min(tuned_never) == max(tuned_never) else pct(min(tuned_never)) + " to " + pct(max(tuned_never))` against `{python} pct(bn["prior-year giving"]["recall"])` for the ranking, a gain whose interval still includes zero. The next section compares the four directly and chooses between them.

## Model Comparison and Selection

This section compares the four tuned models and two ensembles of them, then picks one model with rules set before the comparison was run.

### Candidates

The four tuned models are the L1 and L2 logistic regressions, the explainable boosting machine, and XGBoost, each trained on the FY2014 window with its chosen feature set and the settings average precision picked. Two ensembles are added, which need no new fitting. Each averages the models' ranks within a cohort, so that scores on different scales count equally:

- **All four models**, the broadest average.
- **L1 logistic regression and the explainable boosting machine**, the two most different approaches: one coefficient per feature against one learned curve per feature.

### Selection Rules

The rules were set before the comparison:

1. **Simplicity order.** L1 logistic regression (the fewest active inputs, one coefficient each), then L2 logistic regression (every input kept, one coefficient each), then the explainable boosting machine (a curve per feature plus pairwise interactions), then XGBoost (hundreds of trees), then the ensembles.
2. **Start from the simplest.** A more complex candidate replaces the current choice only if its recall at 1,000 is higher with a paired 95% interval above zero, for all eligible donors or for never-major donors, and it is not measurably worse for the other group.
3. **No measurable difference keeps the simpler model.**
4. **Explanations do not exclude anyone.** Every candidate can show each donor's main drivers in the working queue, through coefficients, the boosting machine's curves, or SHAP values for XGBoost.

```{python}
#| label: candidates

TUNED = {m: tuned_runs[m][0]["average_precision"][0] for m in SHORTLIST}

def rank_average(preds_list, name):
    # average of within-cohort percentile ranks, so models on different score scales count equally
    joined = preds_list[0].rename({"score": "s0"})
    for i, p in enumerate(preds_list[1:], start=1):
        joined = joined.join(p.rename({"score": f"s{i}"}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="inner")
    cols = [f"s{i}" for i in range(len(preds_list))]
    return joined.select("constituent_id", "t", score=pl.mean_horizontal(
        [pl.col(c).rank("average").over("t") / pl.len().over("t") for c in cols])).with_columns(pl.lit(name).alias("_"))\
        .drop("_")

ENSEMBLES = {
    "ensemble: all four": rank_average(list(TUNED.values()), "ensemble: all four"),
    "ensemble: L1 + EBM": rank_average([TUNED["logistic regression (L1)"], TUNED["explainable boosting machine"]],
                                       "ensemble: L1 + EBM"),
}
SIMPLICITY_ORDER = ["logistic regression (L1)", "logistic regression (L2)", "explainable boosting machine", "XGBoost",
                    "ensemble: L1 + EBM", "ensemble: all four"]
candidates = {**TUNED, **ENSEMBLES}
assert set(candidates) == set(SIMPLICITY_ORDER)
assert all(p.height == test_scored.height for p in candidates.values())   # every test donor is scored once

cand_summary, cand_bar_diffs, cand_boots = evaluate_models(candidates)
cand_with = test_scored
for name, p in candidates.items():
    cand_with = cand_with.join(p.rename({"score": f"score__{name}"}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")

def cand_row(g, name):
    return cand_summary.filter((pl.col("group") == g) & (pl.col("ranking") == name)).row(0, named=True)

cd_ = {(r["group"], r["model"], r["versus"]): r for r in cand_bar_diffs.iter_rows(named=True)}
cand_table = pl.DataFrame([
    {"candidate": c,
     "recall_all": cand_row("all eligible", c)["recall"],
     "gain_vs_prior_year": 100 * cd_[("all eligible", c, "prior-year giving")]["difference"],
     "gain_low": 100 * cd_[("all eligible", c, "prior-year giving")]["low"],
     "gain_high": 100 * cd_[("all eligible", c, "prior-year giving")]["high"],
     "recall_never_major": cand_row("never major", c)["recall"],
     "recall_no_contact": cand_row("no contact", c)["recall"],
     "test_average_precision": test_average_precision(f"score__{c}", cand_with)}
    for c in SIMPLICITY_ORDER
])
ct_ = {r["candidate"]: r for r in cand_table.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(cand_table.with_columns(pl.col("gain_vs_prior_year", "gain_low", "gain_high").round(1),
                             pl.col("test_average_precision").round(3)),
     pct_cols=["recall_all", "recall_never_major", "recall_no_contact"],
     caption="Candidates in order of simplicity: recall at 1,000 on the FY2022 to FY2024 test cohorts")
```

```{python}
#| label: selection

# rules 2 and 3, applied in order of simplicity
current = SIMPLICITY_ORDER[0]
selection_log = []
for challenger in SIMPLICITY_ORDER[1:]:
    d_all = paired_difference(cand_boots["all eligible"], challenger, current)
    d_never = paired_difference(cand_boots["never major"], challenger, current)
    wins = (d_all["low"] > 0 and d_never["high"] >= 0) or (d_never["low"] > 0 and d_all["high"] >= 0)
    selection_log.append({
        "challenger": challenger, "current_choice": current,
        "all_gain": 100 * d_all["difference"], "all_low": 100 * d_all["low"], "all_high": 100 * d_all["high"],
        "never_major_gain": 100 * d_never["difference"], "never_major_low": 100 * d_never["low"],
        "never_major_high": 100 * d_never["high"], "replaces_current": bool(wins),
    })
    if wins:
        current = challenger
SELECTED = current
selection_log = pl.DataFrame(selection_log)
show(selection_log.with_columns(pl.col("^.*_(gain|low|high)$").round(1)),
     caption="Selection, step by step: each challenger against the current choice, paired differences in recall at 1,000 (percentage points)")
```

### Strengths and Weaknesses

| Candidate | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| L1 logistic regression | Uses only the inputs that carry signal, with one coefficient each, so it is the easiest to explain to development staff. Fast to fit and to score. | Each feature pushes the odds in one direction only, so curved or threshold effects have to come from the log transform. No interactions unless they are built as features. |
| L2 logistic regression | Same form as L1, and steadier when inputs are correlated, since it shares weight across them. | Keeps every input, so the coefficients are harder to read when correlated inputs split the weight between them. |
| Explainable boosting machine | Learns a curve for each feature and a few pairwise interactions, and shows each donor's contributions directly. | The slowest to tune by far, and its curves are more to explain than one number per feature. Its gain over the regressions did not appear on the test cohorts. |
| XGBoost | The most flexible, finding interactions on its own, and competitive once heavily regularized. | Overfits at ordinary settings with this few converters, is sensitive to tuning, and needs SHAP values to explain a donor's score. |
| Ensembles | The highest recall and average precision, by a small margin, since averaging smooths out each model's errors. | Every component model has to be fit, maintained, and explained, for a gain of about one converter over three years. |

: Strengths and weaknesses of the candidates

### Selected Model

Under the rules, the **L1 logistic regression** is the final model. No challenger beats it measurably. The L2 version differs by `{python} f'{sel["logistic regression (L2)"]["all_gain"]:.1f}'` points of recall for all eligible donors, the boosting machine and XGBoost by `{python} f'{sel["explainable boosting machine"]["all_gain"]:.1f}'` and `{python} f'{sel["XGBoost"]["all_gain"]:.1f}'`, and the ensembles by `{python} f'{sel["ensemble: all four"]["all_gain"]:+.1f}'` (95% interval `{python} f'{sel["ensemble: all four"]["all_low"]:.1f}'` to `{python} f'{sel["ensemble: all four"]["all_high"]:.1f}'` for the four-model ensemble). The ensembles have the highest recall, at `{python} pct(ct_["ensemble: all four"]["recall_all"])`, but on the test cohorts that edge amounts to about `{python} n(round((ct_["ensemble: all four"]["recall_all"] - ct_["logistic regression (L1)"]["recall_all"]) * by_cohort["converters"].sum()))` converter over three years, far inside the noise.

The selected model holds `{python} pct(ct_["logistic regression (L1)"]["recall_all"])` of next-year converters in its top 1,000, `{python} f'{ct_["logistic regression (L1)"]["gain_vs_prior_year"]:.1f}'` points above the prior-year ranking (95% interval `{python} f'{ct_["logistic regression (L1)"]["gain_low"]:.1f}'` to `{python} f'{ct_["logistic regression (L1)"]["gain_high"]:.1f}'`), and it also clears the former major or $500 rule. For never-major donors every candidate, including the selected one, holds `{python} pct(ct_["logistic regression (L1)"]["recall_never_major"])`, which suggests they all find the same never-major converters and miss the same ones. That is `{python} pp(cd_[("never major", SELECTED, "prior-year giving")]["difference"], 1)` points above the prior-year ranking, but the interval (`{python} pp(cd_[("never major", SELECTED, "prior-year giving")]["low"], 1)` to `{python} pp(cd_[("never major", SELECTED, "prior-year giving")]["high"], 1)`) includes zero, so the model does not clear the never-major bar. On the no-contact pool, where officer selection is the comparison, it holds `{python} pct(ct_["logistic regression (L1)"]["recall_no_contact"])` against `{python} pct(nc["officer selection"]["recall"])` for officers and `{python} pct(nc["prior-year giving"]["recall"])` for the prior-year ranking.

Beyond the rules, the choice suits the business problem. A list that development staff work from has to be explainable, and one coefficient per input is the plainest explanation available. The model also fits in `{python} f'{rt_["logistic regression (L1)"]["final_fit_seconds"]:.0f}'` seconds and scores a cohort in under a second, so it can be refit every year without special infrastructure.

## Best Model Performance

### The Final Model

The selected model is an L1-penalized logistic regression on the group EDA's use list, trained on cohorts from FY2014 onward. This section reports its performance in three settings: on the cohorts it was trained on (in-sample), on the FY2022 to FY2024 rolling test (out-of-sample, the basis for every choice so far), and once on the FY2025 cohort, which had been held back from every comparison. Three rules were set before the FY2025 cohort was scored:

1. **The FY2025 check cannot change the model.** It is a check, not a selection. Whatever it shows, the selected model stays, and a weak result is reported as a risk.
2. **Calibration.** If the model's average predicted probability on the test cohorts is more than 25% above or below the observed conversion rate (a ratio outside 0.8 to 1.25), the probabilities get a one-parameter intercept correction estimated on the most recent labeled training cohort. That correction changes the probabilities staff would see but never the order of the list. Inside that range the probabilities are reported as they are.
3. **The penalty strength** of each fitted model is chosen by inner cross-validation on that model's own training cohorts, as in every test so far.

Two models are fit this way. The check model trains on FY2014 to FY2024 and scores the FY2025 cohort. The final model trains on FY2014 to FY2025, every cohort with a known 12 month outcome, and is the one that would score next year's list.

```{python}
#| label: final-fits

import joblib

FINAL_SPEC = chosen_spec(SELECTED, TUNE_START)
FINAL_GRID = TUNE_GRIDS[SELECTED]

def fit_final(train_end, spec=None, grid=None, target="y_12m", train_start=None):
    """Tune by inner cross-validation on train_start to train_end, then fit on all of it.

    Defaults to the selected 12 month model on the FY2014 window. The tuning (the slow part) is cached;
    the final fit with the chosen setting is redone each time, so the fitted pipeline never has to be
    saved to disk.
    """
    spec, grid = spec or FINAL_SPEC, grid or FINAL_GRID
    train_start = TUNE_START if train_start is None else train_start
    key_parts = ["final", CACHE_VERSION, spec["name"], repr(spec["model"]), spec["features"],
                 train_start, train_end, [str(g) for g in grid]]
    if target != "y_12m":
        key_parts.append(target)   # appended only for other outcomes, so the 12 month keys are unchanged
    key = hashlib.sha1(json.dumps(key_parts, default=str).encode()).hexdigest()[:16]
    tuning_path, meta_path = CACHE_DIR / f"final_{key}_tuning.parquet", CACHE_DIR / f"final_{key}_meta.json"
    train = frame.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(train_start, train_end) & pl.col(target).is_not_null())
    if not RERUN and tuning_path.exists() and meta_path.exists():
        tuning_tbl, meta = pl.read_parquet(tuning_path), json.loads(meta_path.read_text())
    else:
        start = perf_counter()
        tuning_tbl = tune(spec, grid, train, target=target)
        meta = {"tune_seconds": perf_counter() - start, "best": pick(tuning_tbl, "average_precision")}
        CACHE_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
        tuning_tbl.write_parquet(tuning_path)
        meta_path.write_text(json.dumps(meta))
    params = grid[[str(g) for g in grid].index(meta["best"])]
    model = clone(spec["model"]).set_params(**params)
    if "random_state" in model.get_params():
        # the liblinear solver shuffles rows; a fixed seed makes the reported coefficients reproducible
        model.set_params(random_state=SEED)
    fitted_spec = {**spec, "model": model}
    X, cols = design(train, fitted_spec["features"])
    # models without a preprocessing pipeline (the boosting machine) are slow to refit and can be saved,
    # so their fitted estimator is cached too; the pipelines refit in seconds
    est_path = CACHE_DIR / f"final_{key}_estimator.joblib"
    if not spec["scaled"] and not RERUN and est_path.exists() and "fit_seconds" in meta:
        est, fit_seconds = joblib.load(est_path), meta["fit_seconds"]
    else:
        est = build(fitted_spec, cols)
        start = perf_counter()
        fit_model(est, X, train[target].cast(pl.Int8).to_numpy())
        fit_seconds = perf_counter() - start
        if not spec["scaled"]:
            joblib.dump(est, est_path)
            meta_path.write_text(json.dumps({**meta, "fit_seconds": fit_seconds}))
    return {"estimator": est, "columns": cols, "params": params, "tuning": tuning_tbl, "train_end": train_end,
            "features": fitted_spec["features"], "training_rows": train.height,
            "training_converters": int(train[target].sum()),
            "tune_seconds": meta["tune_seconds"], "fit_seconds": fit_seconds}

def score_with(fitted, df):
    # probabilities for df's donors with the contact flags off, and the time it took
    X, _ = design(scoring_view(df), FINAL_SPEC["features"])
    start = perf_counter()
    p = predict_score(fitted["estimator"], X)
    return df.select("constituent_id", "t").with_columns(score=pl.Series(p)), perf_counter() - start

check_model = fit_final(2024)   # scores the FY2025 cohort once
final_model = fit_final(2025)   # every cohort with a known 12 month outcome
```

### In-Sample and Out-of-Sample Performance

The table compares the selected model with the two bars in three settings. In-sample is the check model scored on the FY2014 to FY2024 cohorts it was trained on. Out-of-sample is the rolling test from the previous sections, where each test cohort was scored by a model trained only on earlier cohorts. The FY2025 check is the check model scored on a cohort it never saw, whose outcomes fall in FY2026, the first year without federal funding.

```{python}
#| label: performance

def no_contact_pool(df, cohorts):
    # contacted donors dropped and held-out donors reweighted, as in the Benchmarks section
    held = (clean["cultivation"].filter(pl.col("fiscal_year").is_in(cohorts))
            .group_by(t=pl.col("fiscal_year").cast(pl.Int32)).agg(w_held=pl.len() / pl.col("holdout").sum()))
    return (df.filter(~pl.col("contacted")).join(held, on="t", how="left")
            .with_columns(w=pl.when(pl.col("held_out")).then(pl.col("w_held")).otherwise(pl.lit(1.0)),
                          officer=pl.col("held_out").cast(pl.Int32)))

def mean_average_precision(df, col):
    # average precision within each cohort, averaged over cohorts
    return float(np.mean([average_precision_score(d["y"].cast(pl.Int8).to_numpy(), d[col].to_numpy())
                          for d in df.partition_by("t")]))

PERF_SPECS = {"model": "model_score", "prior-year giving": "prior_total", "former major or $500": "rule_former_or_500"}

def performance(setting, df, pred):
    d = df.join(pred.rename({"score": "model_score"}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
    b_all, b_never = bootstrap(d, PERF_SPECS), bootstrap(d.filter(~pl.col("former_major")), PERF_SPECS)
    g_all = paired_difference(b_all, "model", "prior-year giving")
    g_never = paired_difference(b_never, "model", "prior-year giving")
    g_rule = paired_difference(b_all, "model", "former major or $500")
    r, p, l = b_all["point"]["model"]
    lo, hi = np.quantile(b_all["draws"]["model"][:, 0], [0.025, 0.975])
    return {"setting": setting, "cohorts": f"FY{d['t'].min()} to FY{d['t'].max()}" if d["t"].n_unique() > 1 else f"FY{d['t'].min()}",
            "converters": int(d["y"].sum()), "recall": r, "recall_low": lo, "recall_high": hi,
            "precision": p, "lift": round(l, 1), "prior_year_recall": b_all["point"]["prior-year giving"][0],
            "gain": 100 * g_all["difference"], "gain_low": 100 * g_all["low"], "gain_high": 100 * g_all["high"],
            "gain_vs_rule": 100 * g_rule["difference"], "gain_vs_rule_low": 100 * g_rule["low"],
            "never_major_recall": b_never["point"]["model"][0],
            "never_major_prior_year": b_never["point"]["prior-year giving"][0],
            "never_major_gain": 100 * g_never["difference"], "never_major_gain_low": 100 * g_never["low"],
            "never_major_gain_high": 100 * g_never["high"],
            "average_precision": mean_average_precision(d, "model_score"),
            "prior_year_average_precision": mean_average_precision(d, "prior_total")}

fy25 = scored.filter(pl.col("t") == 2025)
fy25_pred, fy25_seconds = score_with(check_model, fy25)
in_sample = scored.filter(pl.col("t").is_between(TUNE_START, 2024))
in_sample_pred, _ = score_with(check_model, in_sample)

perf = pl.DataFrame([
    performance("in-sample (check model on its training cohorts)", in_sample, in_sample_pred),
    performance("out-of-sample (rolling test)", test_scored, TUNED[SELECTED]),
    performance("FY2025 check (held out until now)", fy25, fy25_pred),
])
pf = {r["setting"].split(" (")[0]: r for r in perf.iter_rows(named=True)}
show(perf.select("setting", "cohorts", "converters", "recall", "recall_low", "recall_high", "precision", "lift",
                 "prior_year_recall", "gain", "gain_low", "gain_high", "never_major_recall", "never_major_gain",
                 "average_precision").with_columns(pl.col("gain", "gain_low", "gain_high", "never_major_gain").round(1),
                                                    pl.col("average_precision").round(3)),
     pct_cols=["recall", "recall_low", "recall_high", "precision", "prior_year_recall", "never_major_recall"],
     caption="Selected model: recall at 1,000 in-sample, out-of-sample, and on the FY2025 check, with the paired gain over the prior-year ranking in percentage points")
```

### Calibration

Staff would see each donor's probability of becoming a major donor next year, so the probabilities should be about right, not just the order. Calibration is checked on the rolling test cohorts by comparing the average predicted probability with the observed conversion rate, overall and by position in the ranking.

```{python}
#| label: calibration

def calibration_by_band(df, score_col):
    # predicted and observed conversion by position in the ranking, pooled over cohorts
    bands = [(1, 100), (101, 250), (251, 500), (501, 1000), (1001, 2000), (2001, 5000), (5001, None)]
    ranked_df = df.with_columns(position=pl.col(score_col).rank("ordinal", descending=True).over("t"))
    rows = []
    for lo, hi in bands:
        sel_ = ranked_df.filter(pl.col("position") >= lo) if hi is None else ranked_df.filter(pl.col("position").is_between(lo, hi))
        rows.append({"ranks": f"{lo:,} and below" if hi is None else f"{lo:,} to {hi:,}", "donor_years": sel_.height,
                     "converters": int(sel_["y"].sum()), "mean_predicted": sel_[score_col].mean(),
                     "observed_rate": sel_["y"].mean()})
    return pl.DataFrame(rows)

def brier(df, score_col):
    y = df["y"].cast(pl.Float64).to_numpy()
    return float(np.mean((df[score_col].to_numpy() - y) ** 2)), float(np.mean((y.mean() - y) ** 2))

cal_ratio = {t: float(d["model_score"].sum() / d["y"].sum()) for (t,), d in oos_df.group_by("t")}
pooled_ratio = float(oos_df["model_score"].sum() / oos_df["y"].sum())
NEEDS_RECALIBRATION = not (0.8 <= pooled_ratio <= 1.25)   # rule 2
cal_bands = calibration_by_band(oos_df, "model_score")
brier_model, brier_base = brier(oos_df, "model_score")
fy25_df = fy25.join(fy25_pred.rename({"score": "model_score"}), on=["constituent_id", "t"], how="left")
fy25_ratio = float(fy25_df["model_score"].sum() / fy25_df["y"].sum())
show(cal_bands, pct_cols=["mean_predicted", "observed_rate"], pct_digits=2,
     caption="Calibration on the FY2022 to FY2024 test cohorts: predicted and observed next-year conversion by position in the ranking")
```
